name: assertion
intent: Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions.
problem: Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. A caller can violate a precondition or an operation can break an invariant, allowing invalid state to propagate until an unrelated reader fails; if the assertion is elided by the build, the shipped program may enforce a different contract from the one tested.
context: Objects with genuine invariants - entities, value objects and aggregate roots - whose state changes through several operations or paths, in a language with an assertion facility, contract syntax or an exception mechanism. The invariant must be expressible as a deterministic, side-effect-free predicate over observable state. Use assertions for programmer/model defects; use always-on validation or typed errors for expected input failures, and decide explicitly whether a release build may elide the check.
benefits: Invalid state is caught where it is created: the failure points at the operation that broke the invariant, not at a distant reader much later.
The invariant becomes an executable, nameable predicate that code, tests and diagnostics reuse, instead of prose that no tool evaluates and no refactoring keeps true.
The rule is stated in the language of the model, so a reader sees the contract inside the code and does not have to trust a comment.

Blame is assigned: a failed precondition is the caller's bug, a failed postcondition or invariant is the object's own bug (Meyer's contract model), which turns a wrong value into an actionable defect report.
Checks can be compiled out: with debug-only facilities the invariant costs nothing in production while still being exercised by every debug run and test.
Refactoring safety: a rewrite that would break the invariant fails immediately, which makes aggressive changes to the model cheaper.

Contracts serve double duty as specification and test oracle: a property-based testing harness can feed random inputs satisfying preconditions and assert postconditions hold, while a formal prover (e.g. AutoProof with SMT) can attempt compile-time proof that violations are impossible for all inputs.

DbC transforms fuzzing: a fuzzer that finds a contract violation produces a precise machine-generated report of exactly which invariant was broken and what input caused it, rather than a crash dump requiring reverse engineering.
tradeoffs: Coverage is an obligation, not a property of the pattern: any path that mutates the object outside a check site still corrupts it silently, and the invariant is only as good as the set of guarded transitions.

Build-configuration dependence: NDEBUG, missing -ea, Python -O, Debug.Assert in release, Swift assert in -O and Rust debug_assert! all silently remove the check, so the same code enforces the invariant in debug and ignores it in production.

An assertion is not a validation mechanism: using it for expected user input turns a normal error path into an abort or an AssertionError, and Meyer's contract model explicitly separates correctness conditions from input checking.
Predicates must be side-effect free because they may not be evaluated at all, and expensive invariants (deep graph or collection checks) are unaffordable on every guarded operation.
Extra code at every mutation site inflates constructors and mutators and invites boilerplate invariant() methods that drift away from the state they claim to describe.
Failure modes differ per runtime (abort, exception, panic, trap, message box); code that catches or ignores the violation turns the fail-fast guarantee into silent corruption.

In async or concurrent contexts, a panic in a Rust async task or Java thread does not crash the process but silently kills that task and drops the request - monitoring shows green while availability craters.
Promoting an invariant to production-only checking (always-on exception) while the language strips it creates a divergence between tested code and shipped code.

participants.responsibility: The boolean expression or named predicate method that states what must be true of the object's state, written without side effects so it can be evaluated or compiled out at will.
The constructor or mutator that must establish or preserve the invariant and therefore carries the check at entry (precondition) and/or at exit (postcondition).
The object (or aggregate root) that owns the state and therefore owns its invariants; it decides which states are legal, so the predicate belongs to it.
The exact point where the predicate is evaluated: construction, method entry, method exit, or an invariant hook invoked by every public operation.

The failure mechanism - assertion failure, dedicated exception, abort, panic - which must stay loud and uncaught, because a violated assertion means the program is no longer operating on a valid model.

The invariant predicate reused as a test oracle: property-based testing harnesses feed random inputs satisfying preconditions and assert the postcondition or invariant holds, turning the same predicate into the correctness test.

use_cases: Entities and value objects with cross-field rules: an amount that always carries its currency and scale, a date range whose end follows its start, an order whose total equals the sum of its lines.
Aggregate roots that enforce consistency across a cluster of objects: the root asserts its invariant before accepting a change and after applying it.
Domain services and application services checking the preconditions of a use-case operation, so a mis-wired caller fails on the spot instead of writing corrupt state.
Library and framework code that must state its contract: precondition checks on public constructors and methods that clients cannot legitimately violate.
Legacy models under refactoring: assertions turn implicit rules into explicit ones, and where the language strips assertions the same predicates are pasted into the test suite (Evans's fallback).
Reconstitution code that rebuilds objects from stored data, asserting that persisted state still satisfies the model's invariants before the object is used.

Event-sourced aggregates: each state-transition command asserts the preconditions before applying the event, and the event handler asserts the invariant after the state is reconstituted from the event stream.
CQRS write models: the command handler asserts that the incoming command is valid for the current aggregate state before persisting, catching mis-wired or concurrent commands at the write edge.

Microservice boundary contracts: the inbound adapter asserts the precondition of the domain operation before dispatching, preventing malformed commands from entering the domain core regardless of which transport delivered them (HTTP, queue, gRPC).

Money and quantity types: value objects that wrap a numeric amount and a currency/unit, asserting that amounts are non-negative and operations preserve currency matching, preventing silent unit-mixing bugs.
Workflow or saga state machines: assertions on transition preconditions (this status can only advance to that one) prevent illegal state progression from corrupted or out-of-order events.

Property-based test oracle: postconditions double as generative test properties - for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the postcondition holds - turning the same predicate into a specification that a property-based testing library (e.g. Eris for PHP, Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) can falsify.

EiffelBase container classes such as LINKED_LIST and HASH_TABLE: EiffelStudio contract monitoring checks exported-routine preconditions/postconditions and class invariants while the containers preserve their representation rules.
AutoProof-verified Eiffel classes: executable assertions also serve as formal specifications that the verifier can discharge or flag, pairing runtime diagnostics with static proof where available.
avoid_when: The condition is expected to be false in normal operation - invalid user input or untrusted payloads: use boundary validation or a guard clause that returns a typed error; an Assertion reports a broken contract instead.
The rule can be enforced by construction - non-null types, newtypes, private setters, immutable values, sealed hierarchies: use Make Illegal States Unrepresentable rather than a runtime check.
The condition is expensive to evaluate on every mutation: check it in tests, CI or a consistency job, or put a debug-only assertion on the hot path only after profiling.
The rule is a selection or reporting predicate over objects rather than a property of one object's state: use Specification; Assertion belongs to the state owner.
You need to collect several expected failures into one diagnostic or fluent API: use an Assertion Builder or notification-style validator; this pattern fails fast at the first broken contract.
The check would only restate what the compiler already guarantees (null checks under non-null types, exhaustive matches).

The object is being reconstituted from an ORM or deserialization layer that bypasses constructors: assert in a separate validity method called after hydration completes, not in a constructor that was bypassed.
The only consumer is a test expectation about output or interactions: use the test framework's assertion API; this pattern documents and enforces a production object's contract.
anti_patterns: Wrong move: leave the invariant only in a comment or wiki -> Failure: no constructor or mutator evaluates it, so invalid state propagates until a distant reader fails -> Instead: keep one named predicate on the state owner and invoke it at construction and every state transition.

Wrong move: use assert(amount > 0) for a user or network command -> Failure: invalid input becomes AssertionError/abort, and an optimized build may accept it -> Instead: validate at the boundary with a guard clause or schema validator and return a typed error; reserve assertions for broken internal contracts.

Wrong move: put counter++, cache initialization or another mutation inside an assertion -> Failure: -O/NDEBUG/-ea-disabled removes the work and changes program state -> Instead: perform required work unconditionally, then assert the side-effect-free result.

Catching the violation: an except AssertionError / catch (AssertionError) block that logs and continues -> Failure: the model remains invalid after the check has reported corruption -> Instead: fail the operation and repair or discard the object at an explicit boundary.

Invariant checks that live only in tests while the production object has no guard -> Failure: the verified path and the shipped path are different code -> Instead: keep the named predicate beside the state and call it from production transitions, with tests exercising the same path.

Relying on a disabled assertion for a correctness-critical rule -> Failure: the build flag that removes the check removes the guarantee with it -> Instead: use an always-on exception/result or a type-level invariant for production safety.

Panic or assert in async task handlers -> Failure: a Rust Tokio task or Java executor task can die while the request is dropped and metrics stay green -> Instead: return Result/exceptional completion and let the request boundary report the failure.

Using assert() for security-critical checks that are stripped in production -> Failure: a missing authorization or integrity check becomes a bypass -> Instead: use an always-on security decision and treat assertions only as diagnostic checks.

Constructor-only invariant -> Failure: mutators change state without re-checking, so intermediate states escape the invariant -> Instead: establish the invariant in construction and preserve it after every public mutation.

Silent degradation after invariant violation -> Failure: catching the error and falling back to a default or empty state propagates corruption -> Instead: stop, surface the defect, and rebuild from a known-valid state.

Wrong move: mutate the object and then catch an invariant failure to continue -> Failure: the object remains partially updated and later calls observe corruption -> Instead: compute and validate candidate state before committing, then let an invariant violation propagate as an unhandled defect.

Wrong move: use an Assertion Builder or accumulated validation report for an object invariant -> Failure: expected batch diagnostics become a fail-fast crash, or the rule is detached from its state owner -> Instead: use Assertion Builder/notification validation for expected input errors and this pattern for one object's contract.

Wrong move: assume tests with assertions enabled prove production enforcement -> Failure: Python -O, Java without -ea, or NDEBUG builds ship a different program -> Instead: use an always-on guard/exception or type-level invariant for production guarantees, with assertions as supplemental diagnostics.
design_principles: Fail fast and loudly: a violated invariant means the program's model is broken, and continuing produces worse damage than stopping.
Make the implicit explicit: state the rule in code where it is checked, not in prose where nothing enforces it.
Single source of truth per invariant: one named predicate reused by constructor, mutators, tests and diagnostics.
Separation of contract from mechanism: preconditions bind the caller, postconditions and invariants bind the implementer (Meyer's blame assignment).
Keep the rule next to the state it governs; the invariant belongs to the object (or aggregate root) that owns that state.
Do not use assertions for expected errors: validation is a control-flow concern, invariants are a correctness concern.
Distinguish recoverable errors (return Result) from broken invariants (panic/assert): a library that panics on bad input takes away the caller's choice; return Result and let the caller decide.

Contracts are process, not just runtime: even when disabled in production builds, every CI run, fuzz input, and regression test exercises the full contract, so logic errors surface before they reach production.

Prefer making illegal states unrepresentable over checking them: types, newtypes, private constructors, and sealed hierarchies eliminate entire classes of invariant violation before any runtime check is needed.
best_practices: Write invariants as named predicate methods (is_balanced(), check_invariants()) and call them from the assertion site, so the rule reads like domain language instead of an anonymous expression.
Check at construction and after every mutation: the constructor's job is to establish the invariant, each mutator's job is to preserve it.
Keep predicates side-effect free and cheap; contract code should only read and compare state.

Use the always-on mechanism (exceptions, Trace.Assert, precondition) for rules that must hold in production, and debug-only facilities (assert, Debug.Assert, debug_assert!) for internal sanity checks.
Put the offending values in the failure message; an assertion that only says 'invariant violated' wastes the debugging trip it was meant to save.
Never catch an assertion failure to continue; if production must survive the condition, it is validation and belongs before the assertion, not around it.
Where the language strips assertions, mirror each invariant with a test that calls the same predicate, or promote the rule into the type system.
Name predicates to reflect the domain rule they encode: is_balanced(), has_active_subscription(), satisfies_shipping_window() - not check_invariant1 or validate().

Separate boundary validation from domain invariants: validate incoming DTOs and commands with schema validators or guard clauses that return Result/throw typed exceptions; enforce domain invariants in the aggregate using this pattern.
In async contexts (Rust async/Tokio, Java CompletableFuture), never use panic/assert in task bodies that handle requests; return Result and let the boundary convert it to an error response.

Use contracts as property-based test oracles: define postconditions as properties (for all inputs satisfying preconditions, the result satisfies the postcondition) and use a property-based testing library to falsify them automatically.
Combine with Factory: the factory enforces that every construction path goes through validation, and the aggregate's invariant is guaranteed to hold on exit from the factory.

In deserialization/reconstitution paths (ORM hydration, JSON unmarshal), assert the invariant in a separate validate() method called after the data is loaded, not in the constructor that may be bypassed.
For expensive invariants, check in tests and CI, gate with debug-only assert in hot paths, and run a nightly consistency job that exercises the full predicate over all production instances.
sources: Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Chapter 10 'Supple Design', pattern ASSERTIONS (final manuscript p. 179).

Meyer, 'Applying Design by Contract', IEEE Computer 25(10), 1992, and the Design by Contract chapter of Object-Oriented Software Construction - assertions as preconditions, postconditions and class invariants.

https://www.eiffel.org/blog/Finnian%20Reilly/2026/05/finding-billion-user-project-eiffel-how-dbc-catches-security-flaws-rust-misses - xpact case study: CVE regression as contract violations, AutoTest contract-driven test generation, AutoProof SMT formal verification, void safety static guarantee.

https://serard.dev/content/blog/ts-ddd/37-design-by-contract.html - TypeScript @Pre/@Post/@Invariant decorator implementation with @AggregateRoot composition, old() snapshot semantics, property-based testing harness, ContractViolation typed error.
https://serard.dev/content/blog/ts-ddd/31-entity.html - Entity invariants field bridging to @DesignByContract, DDD0103 analyzer rule for declared-but-not-enforced invariants.
https://serard.dev/content/blog/ts-ddd/34-factory.html - Factory pattern enforcing aggregate invariants at construction with Result return type and validated-entity type pattern.

https://github.com/dirnbauer/webconsultant-skills/blob/main/skills/php-modernization/references/contracts-and-invariants.md - PHP: Webmozart\Assert vs native assert() split, property hooks as invariant points (PHP 8.4), Eris property-based testing, Infection mutation testing, PHPStan @phpstan-assert type narrowing.

https://github.com/k2gl/pragmatic-franken/blob/main/docs/adr/0018-input-validation-and-invariants.md - Two-layer validation ADR: input at edges (DTOs with #[Assert] -> 422), domain invariants in core via named constructors and value objects.

https://sklinkert.github.io/go-ddd/tutorial/02-entities/ - Go DDD entity invariants: validated-entity type pattern (ValidatedProduct), constructor establishment, mutation through methods with re-validation, repository boundary enforcing validated type.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/ch09-03-to-panic-or-not-to-panic.html - Rust: panic for broken invariants (programmer errors), Result for expected failures; when to use thiserror (library API) vs anyhow (application propagation); panic in async Tokio tasks silently drops requests.

https://krun.pro/rust-production-error-handling/ - Rust production error handling: thiserror domain error enums, anyhow application error propagation, IntoResponse boundary mapping, never unwrap() in request handlers, structured error logging with {:#}.

related_patterns_notes.specification: selects objects that satisfy an external business predicate; Assertion enforces a state owner's own contract.
related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: names the operations a model offers; Assertion states the conditions those operations must preserve.
related_patterns_notes.side-effect-free-function: supplies a reusable pure predicate; Assertion supplies the check site and violation behavior.
related_patterns_notes.guard-clause: rejects an expected bad path and continues normal error flow; Assertion signals a broken programmer contract.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: owns a consistency boundary across entities; Assertion is one mechanism the aggregate uses to protect it.
related_patterns_notes.make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: prevents invalid states through types or construction; Assertion verifies what the type system cannot express.
related_patterns_notes.fail-fast: is the general policy of stopping on unrecoverable defects; Assertion is one concrete contract check that applies it.
related_patterns_notes.self-encapsulation: controls access to state through the owner; Assertion checks that the encapsulated state remains legal.
related_patterns_notes.factory: centralizes valid construction paths; Assertion verifies or preserves the invariant after construction and mutation.
related_patterns_notes.notification-pattern: accumulates several expected validation failures; Assertion normally reports the first broken contract and stops.
related_patterns_notes.result-type: represents recoverable failures for callers; Assertion represents a violated internal contract that should not be routine control flow.
related_patterns_notes.property-based-testing: generates inputs and evaluates properties; Assertion supplies a postcondition or invariant as the oracle.
related_patterns_notes.contract-testing: checks an external provider/consumer interaction; Assertion checks an in-process object's preconditions, postconditions or invariant.
